newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia central bank to ease policy to spur growth.
newsitem.headline: Croatia central bank to ease policy to spur growth.

text.p: The Croatian central bank, encouraged by good inflation data, wants to relax its grip on money supply to help spur growth, while maintaining macroeconomic stability, the bank's governor said.
Marko Skreb, head of the National Bank of Croatia, told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday he would like to ease reserve requirements for banks and continue with cuts in official interest rates.
"I would like to see the reserve requirement at below 30 percent by the end of this year," he said.
Lowering of the mandatory reserve ratio -- now set at 34.85 percent of all kuna deposits -- will take place in gradual steps after a token cut of one percentage point in April.
The bank recently cut the Lombard and the discount rate to 9.5 and 5.9 percent respectively.

Although it no longer fears immediate spill-over of higher liquidity into consumption, the central bank would probably not act until demand for local money rises this summer due to seasonal hard currency inflows , Skreb said.

In 1995, the reserve ratio was raised to counter ballooning money supply after Croatians switched their under- the-mattress hard currency savings for local money, the kuna, in a sign of confidence in the stabilising economy.

A process of reducing inflation, by freezing wages and limiting public spending, from the roughly 1,200 in the middle of the Yugoslav conflict in 1993 has caused a drastic decline in living standards. It also lowered the amount of money in the economy, making money supply more sensitive to foreign inflows.
The government is now seeking improve living standards through small tax cuts and wage increases.
But Skreb believes these moves, coinciding with the election year, will not revive inflation which should stay at the current levels.
He set 1997 inflation target as "somewhere between three and four percent", against the annual 3.4 percent at the end of December last year and 3.7 percent in 1995.

March retail prices edged up only 0.1 percent on a monthly basis after stagnating in February and 3.9 percent year-on-year. Producer prices fell 0.7 percent from February, rising 2.2 percent from the same month last year.

As part of its efforts to keep money supply in check, the central bank plans to keep lending to the government at a low level, now approximately 10 percent of the ceiling set at five percent of the budget.

Skreb said that there was no need to revamp the bank's exchange rate policy of keeping the kuna fairly stable even though the bank was considering measures to prevent its appreciation at times of greater tourism-boosted foreign inflows.
The kuna is little changed from its launch three years ago at 6.0 to the dollar and 3.7 against the German mark.
"The kuna will (continue) to be allowed to float freely with some interventions on the foreign exchange market," he said, firmly ruling out any possibility of its devaluation to boost exports.

The central bank usually buys more hard currency from money changers and commercial banks when demand for local currency peaks during the summer tourist season, and hopes to boost its international reserves by $450-500 million this year.

Foreign inflows constitute the main source of money supply, forcing the central bank to increase kuna liquidity. But this year the pressure should weaken compared with last year when money supply rose almost 40 percent.
Skreb said the bank would continue to closely watch the effect of capital inflows, particularly the poorly monitored direct foreign investment, in case of a need to counter them.
"A larger privatisation project may require additional sterilisation measures. Maintaining stability is a goal that must never be forgotten, however boring it may sound," he said.

Separately, the central bank would introduce the Croatian payments system to the last Serb-held enclave of Eastern Slavonia -- a move intended to integrate the region under Zagreb's rule sometime this year.
Converting an equivalent of some 200 million kuna in other currencies, estimated to circulate in the region, was not regarded as a threat to the overall financial stability.

Skreb said that although the easing up of monetary policy should help commercial banks reduce lending rates, there were structural reasons preventing an increase in much-needed credit action for investment.
"... the problem is a structural one and does not lie in money supply," Skreb said.
The governor listed low capital, over-staffing and lack of modern banking services as the main weaknesses of the banking sector.
He said, however, that tougher competition and likely mergers of smaller domestic banks with foreign would gradually increase the sector's efficiency.
